title: Do Good Leaders Ever Act Aggressively
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay distinguishes assertiveness from aggression, arguing the two are frequently conflated but are actually quite distinct. Assertive leaders state their views confidently while respecting others' needs and boundaries; aggressive leaders force their will through disrespect, intimidation, or coercion. The piece catalogs concrete aggressive tactics -- sarcasm, shouting, staring down, implied threats -- and warns that even well-intentioned leaders can slip into aggression under high-stakes pressure, creating a habit that's easy to repeat. It concludes that sustained respect for self and others is what keeps assertive leaders from crossing the line.
points: Assertiveness and aggression are distinctly different, not points on the same spectrum -- assertive leaders persuade, aggressive leaders coerce.
Aggressive tactics include cutting sarcasm, shouting, invading personal space, interrupting, and implied threats.
High-stakes, emotionally charged situations can push even well-intentioned leaders into aggression without their noticing.
Acting aggressively once and getting the desired result makes it easier to repeat the behavior in the future.
Respect -- for self and others -- is the discipline that keeps a leader assertive rather than aggressive.
quotes: The line between acting assertively and behaving aggressively is not as thin as most leaders believe.
Assertive leaders are forthright about their wants and needs, making it perfectly clear they hold a view or position they believe is right.
To get their way, aggressive leaders turn to cutting sarcasm, shouting, invading personal space, barbs and insults, interrupting, implied threats, talking over others, or staring others down.
Once they act aggressively and get their way, it becomes easier for them to engage with hostility in the future.
Aggression is always disrespectful, so it is the giving of respect that prevents good leaders from becoming inappropriately aggressive, rather than assertive.
